title: 68 Educating producers to reduce anthelmintic resistance in small ruminants
content:
Abstract
The management of internal parasites, most notably Haemonchus contortus (barber pole worm), is widely considered to be the greatest challenge for small ruminant producers. Anthelmintic resistance has been observed worldwide in all available classes of dewormers, making internal parasite management especially difficult and a leading threat to small ruminant industries. In Florida, this challenge is exacerbated by a warm and humid climate that favors parasite function and growth nearly year-round. County extension agents collaborated with university specialists to offer targeted training opportunities for producers to gain the skills and knowledge needed to use anthelmintics in accordance with research-based recommendations and selectively treat animals for internal parasites, with the goal of improving internal parasite management and slowing the development of drug resistance. To accomplish this, the FAMACHA system was taught through a producer certification program. FAMACHA scoring is a standardized, widely accepted practice involving recognizing anemia associated with Haemonchus contortus infection by examining and classifying the color of mucous membranes in the eye, allowing the producer to identify animals to be treated. The certification program is composed of an online module, exam, and in-person lecture, demonstration, and hands-on training. Since 2022, six FAMACHA certification programs have been offered to 148 individuals. Program surveys indicated 91% of participants increased their knowledge across the various topics presented, and 30 surveyed individuals indicated a total economic benefit of $21,499 as a result of the course. Additionally, 85% of respondents indicated an intention to change their behavior to include at least one of the following practices: monitoring the flock or herd for internal parasites, deworming according to research-based recommendations, and utilizing the FAMACHA method. The certification process gives producers the confidence to effectively conduct FAMACHA scoring on their operations, reducing their use of veterinary services, and tailoring deworming treatments to those animals who truly need it, while reducing overall dewormer use for the flock or herd. Overall, this benefits the producer by reducing operational expenses and maintaining livestock health, while also positively impacting small ruminant industries by working toward slowing the development of anthelminthic resistance.
